手風琴以風袋推拉使氣流通過黃銅或鋼簧片發聲，按鍵或按鈕開啟氣門；音量由風袋推拉與: The accordion sounds by pushing and pulling the bellows so that air passes through brass or steel reeds, with keys or buttons opening the pallets; the volume is controlled by the movement of the bellows and the opening of the pallets, and the valves on the opposing reeds reduce leakage and make the sound louder. The range varies with the number of keys, buttons and register switches. The right hand plays the melody and the left accompanies with bass notes or preset chord buttons, so that melody and accompaniment come from one instrument. The related concertina, harmonica and bandoneon do not have this dual melody-and-accompaniment character; the harmonium and the American reed organ are free-reed aerophones too, but larger and set on the floor or a table.

It also appears in Cajun, zydeco, jazz and klezmer, and in classical solo and orchestral writing; many European conservatories have a classical accordion department.

The accordion is a box-shaped free-reed aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 412.132 / 412.132-62-8. The player works the bellows and plays the melody on keys or buttons on the right and the accompaniment on bass or preset chord buttons on the left; air passing the reeds makes the sound. It belongs to the free-reed aerophone family, along with the harmonica, concertina and bandoneon. Spread by European emigrants, it is used in popular music such as chamamé, vallenato, merengue and norteño, and also in dance music, folk music, Cajun, zydeco, jazz, klezmer, and classical solo and orchestral music.
手風琴為風袋驅動的自由簧氣鳴樂器，名稱源自19世紀德語Akkordeon。基本形: The accordion is a bellows-driven free-reed aerophone, its name from the nineteenth-century German Akkordeon. The basic form is believed to have been invented by Buschmann of Berlin in 1822, and in 2006 an instrument thought to be earlier was found. In 1829 Demian took out a patent in Vienna on an instrument with only a left-hand keyboard that could sound a chord with one button and had a double-acting reed system. It reached Britain around 1828 and was reported in The Times in 1831, and was popular in New York in the 1840s; in 1830 Sizov and Vorontsov in Tula, Russia, began making them, and production later became large. In 1844 Wheatstone took out a patent on the concertina, and in 1854 Müller wrote a book recording the many varieties.
手風琴的發聲體為自由簧，來源指出簧片為黃銅或鋼製薄片，置於簧框中，氣流通過時振動: The sounding body of the accordion is a free reed; the source says the reeds are thin plates of brass or steel set in a reed frame, vibrating when air passes. The instrument also has valves on the opposing reeds, to reduce leakage and increase the volume. It is played by compressing or expanding the air with the bellows, while keys or buttons on the right and bass or preset chord buttons on the left open the pallets. The source does not state the specific materials of the other parts — the body, bellows, key tops, buttons, reed frames and pallets — so nothing is assumed here.
演奏手風琴時，演奏者以右手按鍵盤或按鈕奏旋律，以左手按貝斯或預設和弦按鈕伴奏，同: To play the accordion, the right hand plays the melody on the keyboard or buttons and the left hand accompanies on the bass or preset chord buttons, while the bellows are compressed or expanded so that air passes the reeds. A beginner can first practise coordinating the direction of the bellows with the keys, since some accordions have a double-acting reed system and the same key may sound a different pitch when the bellows are pulled and when they are pushed. The bellows are also the main means of controlling the attack and the articulation.
